case_name: South Korea Sejong City AI Smart City Platform
problem_solved: Sejong was Korea's purpose-built administrative capital (pop 400,000) designed as a testbed for smart city technologies. The government needed to demonstrate commercial-scale deployment of AI urban management systems — autonomous vehicles, AI traffic management, smart energy grid, digital citizen services — to develop exportable Korean smart city products.
architecture_summary: Sejong Smart City National Pilot Zone: (1) Autonomous Vehicle Corridor — 7.7km fully AV-ready road with 5G + V2X communications; (2) AI Traffic Management — 300+ adaptive signal intersections, incident detection; (3) Energy Management — AI-optimised community energy storage + building management; (4) City Data Hub — all city data on shared platform, API-accessible; (5) 60-minute delivery service (logistics drone pilot). Government investment: $2.5B in infrastructure over 5 years. KOICA exports Sejong model to developing countries as 'K-Smart City'.
outcome_metrics: Traffic efficiency: 20% improvement vs comparable Korean cities. AV test fleet: 40 vehicles in daily operation. Energy consumption: 12% below Korean city average. City data hub: 45 agencies sharing data. K-Smart City exports: 22 cities in 14 countries studying Sejong model. KOICA has 4 active K-Smart City transfer projects.
failure_modes: Cost: $2.5B for 400,000 people — $6,250/resident is unaffordable for most countries. AV system limited to dedicated corridor — cannot scale to irregular urban grid. Energy management AI requires residential smart meter density that took 5 years to achieve.
replicability_factors: KOICA K-Smart City programme transfers specific modules (AI traffic, energy management, data hub) without the full investment. Korean smart city companies (Samsung SDS, LG CNS) active in CA markets. Directly relevant to Tashkent and potential Nurafshan R&D city.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ announced Nurafshan Innovation Centre near Tashkent — a pilot smart city zone. Sejong is the direct reference. Modular adoption: AI traffic ($10-20M) + city data hub ($5-8M) for Tashkent without the $2.5B total investment. KOICA K-Smart City programme is the procurement pathway.
kg_transferability_rationale: Sejong's scale is totally incompatible with KG. Only the AI traffic module ($3-5M for Bishkek) and city data hub concept are applicable. Score 4: aspirational reference, not practical at KG scale.
key_adaptation_required: Modular adoption: AI traffic + city data hub only. Russian/Uzbek interface. Open-source data hub (FIWARE) vs Korean proprietary stack. No AV corridor — premature for CA markets.

problem_solved: Brazil's 26 states and federal government each had separate portals (1,400+ .gov.br domains) with different authentication, UX, and service quality. Citizens needed separate logins for federal social security, driving licence, tax filing, and vaccine certificates. gov.br unified all federal services behind a single authenticated portal.
architecture_summary: Single Sign-On platform using Login.gov.br: CPF (national ID) + password or biometric authentication. Progressive trust levels: Bronze (self-declaration), Silver (bank-verified), Gold (biometric via Serpro ID). Backend: 1,800+ connected federal services. API: gov.br Digital Certificate API used by 300+ private sector companies for KYC. COVID: digital certificate on gov.br saved programme months of time. AI: personalized service recommendations based on citizen profile and life events (birth, death, employment change). Analytics: SEGES dashboard tracking service delivery times across all agencies.
outcome_metrics: 155M registered users (Brazil pop 215M). 4,000+ federal services. Average service completion time: reduced 45%. COVID certificate: 350M issued. Portal digital accessibility: WCAG 2.1 AA certified. Brazil climbed 20 places in UN e-Government Survey after gov.br launch. Life events personalisation: 80% of users receive relevant service suggestions.
failure_modes: State government integration (26 states) lagged federal services by 3 years. Biometric enrollment required in-person for Gold level — excluded 40M rural citizens. Identity theft via CPF-credential theft required multi-factor authentication rollout.
replicability_factors: SERPRO publishes technical documentation. Brazil is an active South-South digital cooperation partner. Login.gov.br architecture is directly comparable to UZ MyID evolution path. Brazil's life event personalisation concept is directly applicable to EPIGU.
uz_transferability_rationale: Brazil's progressive trust level model (Bronze/Silver/Gold) is the right evolution path for UZ MyID — enabling partial access for citizens without full biometric verification while providing full access to those enrolled. The life events personalisation ('proactive government') is the EPIGU evolution UZ officials have stated publicly. Budget: $5-10M on existing EPIGU. UNDP South-South digital cooperation could fund Brazilian-UZ advisory exchange.
kg_transferability_rationale: Brazil's progressive trust level model is highly applicable to KG where rural biometric enrollment coverage is incomplete. Bronze/Silver/Gold layers allow Tunduk services to be accessible even to citizens without GRS biometric card enrollment. Budget: $3-5M.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Uzbek/Kyrgyz language portal. Progressive trust level framework legal decree. Life events API (detecting birth registration, new business registration, etc.) for proactive service suggestions. State/oblast government integration plan from Day 1.

problem_solved: Rwanda, with a population of 13.5M and GDP of $12B, needed to demonstrate that a small, low-income African country could deploy AI at scale in public services. Vision 2050 included AI as a transformative pillar — not for status signalling but to specifically address Rwanda's infrastructure bottlenecks: healthcare access, agricultural productivity, and government service delivery in a mountainous country.
architecture_summary: Rwanda AI Policy 2023: government AI use case registry (50+ approved applications across ministries), National AI Lab (University of Rwanda AI Center), Smart Rwanda Master Plan 2024-2029 including AI infrastructure (400GPU compute available by 2025). Applications in production: Babyl health triage, Irembo digital services (see separate cases), agriculture drone monitoring (crop disease detection via mobile image), e-court pilot (AI transcription). Governance: Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Authority AI ethics committee. Rwanda positioning: 'AI-first small country' as export pitch for other low-income government AI programmes.
outcome_metrics: 50+ government AI applications deployed or in pilot. 400 GPU national compute. University of Rwanda AI Center: 200+ researchers. Rwanda AI readiness index: ranked #2 in Africa (OECD 2024). Export case: 12 African governments have studied Rwanda AI model. WHO cited Rwanda as global reference for low-income country AI in health.
failure_modes: Brain drain: top AI graduates hired by US/UK companies. Budget sustainability: many AI pilots funded by donors with unclear government recurrent budget. Private sector AI adoption lagging public sector. Infrastructure: power reliability (80% electrification) limits AI deployment in rural areas.
replicability_factors: Rwanda's AI-first small country model is the direct comparator for KG. Rwanda publishes case studies via Smart Rwanda Initiative. African Development Bank documents Rwanda model for Africa. UNDP and World Bank explicitly cite Rwanda for small-country AI strategy design.
uz_transferability_rationale: Rwanda is a smaller-economy reference point. Key lesson for UZ: government AI use case registry (50+ approved applications) — UZ MoDT should create a formal registry as governance mechanism. Rwanda's AI ethics committee approach is directly applicable to UZ's AI governance gap.
kg_transferability_rationale: Rwanda (13.5M, $12B GDP) is the closest population and income comparator to KG (6.5M, $12B GDP). Rwanda's three-year progression from 0 to 50+ government AI applications on small budget ($85M over 5 years) is exactly what KG's AI strategy should target. Rwanda-KG South-South learning programme (via UNDP or World Bank) would be high-value.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Kyrgyz language interfaces (Rwanda is French/English/Kinyarwanda). Adaptation for mountain geography vs Rwanda's hill terrain (similar challenges, different scale). Budget recurrence planning — Rwanda's lesson on donor-exit sustainability is critical for KG.

case_name: Kazakhstan Digital Social Protection — e-Otinish Social Registry
problem_solved: Kazakhstan's social protection system distributed benefits to 3M+ recipients through paper applications, physical window visits, and manually verified income declarations. Targeting errors and fraud cost $300M+/year. e-Otinish (e-Application) digitised social benefit applications and created an AI means-testing system that cross-referenced income from 12 government databases.
architecture_summary: e-Otinish platform (Ministry of Labour, ENOF pension fund): online and mobile application for all social benefits (housing, childcare, disability, pension supplements). AI means-testing: income cross-check across tax GNK, pension ENOF, property registry, vehicle registry, banking KQIB data. Application decision: instant pre-decision in 72% of cases; complex cases to officer review. Digital payments: benefits disbursed directly to citizen bank account (IBAN). Fraud analytics: lifestyle-based anomaly detection (declared low income + luxury purchase + overseas travel pattern flagging). Integration with X-Road equivalent (Smart Bridge).
outcome_metrics: 4M+ social benefit applications processed digitally. 72% of applications decided instantly via AI means-testing. Social benefit fraud identified: KZT 28B ($60M) in 3 years. Officer workload per application: reduced 55%. Payment disbursement: same-day bank transfer (vs 15 business days physical). Benefit targeting accuracy: 88% of recipients meet actual eligibility criteria (vs 72% pre-digital).
failure_modes: Means-testing false positives: 12% of legitimate applicants denied due to data errors in source databases. Rural areas without banking access: 15% of benefit recipients still require cash payment infrastructure. Disability certification: AI cannot verify medical conditions — still requires doctor certification creating bottleneck.
replicability_factors: World Bank Social Protection team cites KZ e-Otinish as CIS reference. Russian-language system directly applicable to UZ and KG. UZ World Bank social protection project includes digital registry component.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ social protection reform (World Bank TA) is actively digitising benefits administration. e-Otinish is the direct reference for UZ unified social benefit application (ASA — Agency for Social Assistance). KZ income cross-check architecture maps to UZ MyID + GNK + pension fund integration. Budget: $10-15M. World Bank social protection project is the donor pathway. This is the most directly actionable social protection case in the dataset.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG social protection (UISE — Unified Social Information System) is partially digital but lacks AI means-testing. e-Otinish at KG scale ($5-8M) would dramatically improve targeting and reduce fraud. KG social protection fund reform is an active World Bank project component.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Uzbek/Kyrgyz multilingual interface. Income data cross-check adapted to UZ/KG available databases (less comprehensive than KZ). Cash payment fallback for rural unbanked recipients. Medical certification integration for disability benefits.

case_name: Japan Digital Agency — Post-COVID Government Digitalisation Sprint
problem_solved: Japan's COVID response exposed the consequences of digital neglect: relief payments took 3+ months to reach citizens due to paper-based procedures, fax machines still used between ministries, and My Number (national ID) had 35% enrollment with zero digital utility. Digital Agency was created as a whole-of-government digital transformation unit reporting directly to Cabinet.
architecture_summary: Japan Digital Agency (JDA): Cabinet-level agency with authority over IT standards across all ministries. My Number + My Number Card (physical + digital wallet on iPhone/Android) integration with health insurance, bank accounts, tax, and driver's licence. Digital Common Platform: API-first government system standards (no more legacy custom procurement — all systems must use standard APIs). Government cloud: Government System Standardisation Programme moving 1,700 government systems to cloud by 2025. AI: government-wide LLM policy (civils servants allowed Bing AI/Copilot with government tenant isolation).
outcome_metrics: My Number digital card: 74M issued (60% of population). 1,200 government systems moved to cloud by 2025. Fax machine use: eliminated in 98% of government offices by 2024. COVID digital payments (2022 follow-up): 4 weeks vs 3 months for paper (2020). Government API standardisation: 300+ common APIs defined. JDA won Nikkei Digital Governance Award 2024.
failure_modes: Old-guard resistance: METI and some LDP politicians publicly resisted My Number expansion (privacy concerns). Data breach: MHLW data leak from My Number linkage in 2023 (7.3M records) — required emergency security audit. Speed vs quality: rapid cloud migration created system incompatibilities requiring $400M rework.
replicability_factors: JDA published methodology and lessons. KOICA references JDA for Korean-Japanese parallel approach. The COVID-disaster-driven urgency model (mandate digital before next crisis) is directly applicable to UZ/KG as both face natural disaster digital gaps.
uz_transferability_rationale: Japan's Digital Agency model — Cabinet-level authority over IT standards, cloud mandate, API standardisation — is the governance model UZ MoDT should study. UZ currently lacks the cross-government authority to enforce API standards. The LESSON not the technology: create a Cabinet-level digital authority with real power to mandate standards. Budget: governance change, not technology spend.
kg_transferability_rationale: Japan's model is too large and too expensive for direct KG replication. Key lesson: the UDP digital department (post-April 2026 reorganisation) IS the equivalent of JDA — Presidential Administration-level authority over digital standards. KG should formalize UDP's authority explicitly in the new Положение (regulation) being drafted.
key_adaptation_required: Budget adaptation (Japan $2.8B → UZ $30-50M phased). API standards mandate via Presidential decree. Cloud migration starting with new systems only (legacy migration is too expensive in near term). Governance structure: Cabinet authority for digital standards enforcement.

case_name: Kazakhstan AI for Critical Minerals Exploration (Kazakhmys/Altyntau)
problem_solved: Kazakhstan holds 25% of world's chromite, 30% of manganese, and significant copper/gold deposits. Manual geological survey data interpretation required PhD geophysicists taking 6-18 months per prospect. AI-assisted mineral potential mapping using satellite imagery, historical geological survey data, and geophysical readings could reduce exploration cycle from 5 years to 18 months.
architecture_summary: KazGeology AI platform (MIID — Ministry of Industry and Infrastructural Development): satellite multispectral analysis (Sentinel-2 + ASTER thermal) for surface mineralogy mapping; historical Soviet geological survey data digitisation (30,000+ reports scanned via OCR + NLP extraction); machine learning mineral potential model (random forest on geochemical + geophysical + remote sensing features). Commercial application: Kazakhmys Corporation using platform to prioritise 50+ exploration blocks. KazGeology also provides academic access to model outputs for 7 Central Asian universities.
outcome_metrics: Mineral prospect screening time: 12-week AI assessment vs 2-year traditional survey. 15 new exploration blocks identified with >80% confidence in 3 years. Cost per prospect assessment: 85% reduction. Soviet geological data digitised: 30,000+ documents now machine-readable. Kazakhmys confirmed 3 new copper deposits via AI-prioritised drilling.
failure_modes: Soviet-era geological data quality inconsistency (different standards across decades). Model accuracy drops for deposit types not well-represented in training data. Legal rights to Soviet-era geological data unclear — some data legally contested. Validation drilling cost ($2-5M per prospect) still required to confirm AI predictions.
replicability_factors: Free satellite data (Sentinel-2, ASTER). Kazakhstan's Soviet geological archive digitisation methodology applicable to UZ/KG who have similar archives. KazGeology has bilateral data-sharing protocols with CA neighbours. Critical minerals AI exploration is global trend with major donor interest (US DFC, EBRD).
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ has gold, uranium, copper, molybdenum, and rare earth deposits with significant unexplored potential. Soviet geological archive at GIGEOS (State Institute of Geology) has same structure as Kazakhstan's. AI mineral exploration using free satellite data + digitised Soviet archives is achievable for $3-6M. US DFC (critical minerals financing), EBRD, and ADB are active funders in UZ mining sector.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG has gold (Kumtor and 50+ unexplored deposits), antimony, and rare earths. Soviet geological archive in KG Geological Survey. AI mineral exploration is HIGH PRIORITY under KG's economic strategy. US DFC has specific critical minerals programme for KG. Budget: $3-5M. This is a convergent case: mining + digital + export revenue potential.
key_adaptation_required: Russian-language Soviet archive OCR (similar quality issues as KZ). Adaptation of mineral potential model for KG's metamorphic geology (different from KZ's sedimentary basins). Legal framework for AI-generated prospect data as exploration licence basis. Environmental monitoring integration (avoid AI recommendations in protected areas).
